#657. The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets

Establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon will require more than rockets, habitats, and life support systems. Engineers must also find ways to protect astronauts and equipment from extreme temperatures that can swing from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling hot. Reliable insulation will be essential, but keeping heat under control is only part of the problem.

Materials used in lunar construction must also survive transportation, installation, accidental impacts, and years of handling. Many of the best insulators are surprisingly delicate, making them poorly suited to the demanding conditions of a working Moon base.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania may have found an answer in an unexpectedly familiar material: Mylar. This lightweight plastic is used in everyday products such as food wrap and, when coated with aluminum, the reflective emergency blankets that help marathon runners retain body heat. By arranging hundreds of extremely thin Mylar sheets into carefully designed stacks, the team has created insulation that remains effective even after being bent or subjected to intense pressure.

The research, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, introduces a material known as hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS). Its main advantage is the ability to combine two qualities that are difficult to achieve together: excellent thermal insulation and resistance to physical damage.

"These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression and maintain their insulating performance," says senior author Igor Bargatin, Associate Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM), "potentially allowing them to be packed, transported and survive rough treatment over many years of use."

If engineers can eventually manufacture the material on a large scale, it could be used to protect lunar habitats, spacesuits, and other equipment designed to function for extended periods in the vacuum of space.

"The combination of thermal and mechanical robustness is critical for long-term use on the Moon," notes first author Danielle R. Levin, a recent Penn doctoral graduate in chemistry, who also received a master's in MEAM. "This material could open a pathway to inexpensive, durable and reusable lunar insulation."

Designing insulation for the Moon involves a difficult balancing act. A material must slow the movement of heat through a vacuum while also remaining strong enough to withstand the stresses of everyday use.

Some existing materials are outstanding at preventing heat transfer but offer little protection against physical damage. Aerogels, for instance, consist mostly of empty space, which makes them extremely lightweight and effective at retaining heat. They have been used in applications ranging from industrial pipelines to NASA's Mars rovers. However, their delicate internal structure can make them vulnerable to impacts and compression.

Another widely used space technology, multilayer insulation, relies on reflective sheets separated by insulating spacers. It works particularly well at reducing heat transfer through radiation, but it is not intended to support substantial weight. Even routine contact can cause tearing or other damage.

Strengthening insulation often creates another problem: the changes that make it more durable can also allow more heat to pass through. For future lunar infrastructure, engineers need a material that can resist damage without sacrificing thermal performance.

"For lunar infrastructure, we would ideally like both," says Bargatin. "The ideal material is both resistant to damage and to the loss of heat."

How Ordinary Mylar Became Powerful Space Insulation

The Penn researchers focused on Mylar, a well-known plastic formally called biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate, or BoPET. Already used extensively in aerospace technology, the polymer is also found in the lightweight emergency blankets distributed after marathons. Adding a metallic coating such as aluminum allows Mylar to reflect infrared radiation, helping prevent heat from escaping.

Rather than relying on a single sheet, the researchers investigated what would happen if many thin layers were stacked together. They experimented with different film thicknesses and applied extremely thin coatings of aluminum oxide, also called alumina, to some samples to make the sheets stiffer.

Assembling the experimental stacks was surprisingly difficult. Each delicate film had to be positioned individually, requiring painstaking manual work.

"At the moment, the process is very time-consuming," says Levin. "We use two pairs of tweezers and small weights to handle and stack the delicate films. Even breathing near the stack can send the layers flying."

Despite the simplicity of the basic idea, testing revealed an impressive combination of properties. In a vacuum, the best stacks achieved thermal conductivity comparable to other advanced vacuum insulation materials while retaining their flexibility.

The researchers also tested the material under compression similar to what insulation could experience inside a lunar habitat, where the interior air pressure would push against walls exposed to the vacuum outside.

Additional mechanical testing showed that stacks coated with alumina could tolerate the greatest compressive stresses available with the laboratory equipment while maintaining their insulating performance. The results demonstrated that improving durability did not necessarily require giving up thermal protection.

Crushing Pressure Reveals Unexpected Durability

One of the most striking findings came when the team subjected the material to repeated compression. Even the researchers were surprised by how well the thin plastic layers held up.

The samples were compressed to approximately 20 megapascals, a pressure comparable to concentrating 200 pounds of force onto an area the size of a fingertip. Instead of testing the material only once, the researchers repeated the process 10 times.

"We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress," recalls Levin. "But the stacks didn't survive just one high stress cycle -- they survived 10 in a row."

This resistance to damage could be especially valuable for lunar exploration. Every piece of equipment needed on the Moon must first endure the challenges of being packed, launched, transported, and installed. Insulation that can bend, withstand pressure, and potentially be reused would offer significant practical advantages.

Durability would remain important after construction is complete. Astronauts living and working inside a lunar habitat could accidentally strike or compress insulation during maintenance or ordinary activities.

"You could use these stacks to insulate a lunar habitation, but astronauts will inevitably have little accidents where they bump into them," notes Bargatin. "When we're talking about long-term habitation on the moon, it's really important to have tough materials that can last long enough."

Tiny Particles Reveal a Hidden Secret of Heat Transfer

Beyond demonstrating the material's durability, the experiments uncovered an important clue about how heat travels through layers of Mylar.

The discovery involved microscopic particles already present in commercially manufactured plastic films. Extremely thin sheets naturally tend to stick to one another and to nearby surfaces, which complicates manufacturing and handling. To prevent this, producers add tiny "antiblocking" particles that extend slightly above the plastic surface and keep neighboring sheets from clinging together.

Although manufacturers have long understood why these particles are useful, their influence on heat transfer in stacked Mylar films had received relatively little attention.

Traditional multilayer space insulation is primarily designed to control heat transferred by radiation. As a result, researchers have had less reason to investigate how small points of physical contact between films might affect heat conduction.

The Penn team examined this possibility by constructing mathematical models of heat transfer between individual layers and comparing the predictions with laboratory measurements.

The findings indicate that, in a vacuum, much of the heat moving from one Mylar sheet to the next passes through the tiny contact points created by the antiblocking particles.

That result could have important implications for future insulation design. Instead of accepting the particles as an incidental feature of commercial plastic, engineers might deliberately control their size, abundance, and placement to reduce unwanted heat transfer.

Why Thinner Plastic Does Not Always Insulate Better

The role of these microscopic particles also helped explain another unexpected result.

At first, the researchers assumed that thinner Mylar sheets would produce better insulation. Using thinner films would allow more layers to occupy the same amount of space, increasing the number of boundaries that heat must cross.

However, the experiments did not fully support that expectation. When coated with alumina, the thinnest films the team successfully characterized provided thermal performance similar to films of medium thickness.

The researchers suspect that the antiblocking particles help explain why. In thinner sheets, the particles can produce more contact between adjacent layers, creating additional routes for heat to move through the material. Those extra contact points can offset the expected advantages of adding more layers.

The finding suggests that making films thinner is not automatically the best approach. Engineers must also consider how the sheets bend and deform under pressure, along with the number and arrangement of microscopic contact points.

"As you compress the layers, the contact landscape changes," says Levin. "It's not just a matter of minimizing the film thickness or the number of particles; we must also account for how the contacts change and the films deform as pressure increases."

Ultimately, the ability of these stacks to limit heat transfer depends on several interacting factors, including the thickness and stiffness of the plastic and the distribution of particles within it.

From Tiny Laboratory Samples to Future Moon Bases

Although the early results are encouraging, the new insulation is still far from being ready for lunar construction.

The experimental HyLIFS samples currently measure only about one square centimeter, and producing them requires hours of careful cutting and manual stacking. That painstaking process would be impractical for manufacturing the large sheets needed to insulate an entire habitat.

To make the material useful on a larger scale, the researchers will need a more efficient production method. One possibility involves continuously applying coatings to large rolls of Mylar, using manufacturing techniques that could eventually produce sheets measured in meters rather than centimeters.

Such an approach might also allow engineers to adjust the thickness of the plastic, the protective coatings, and the distribution of antiblocking particles before assembling the material into larger stacks.

Important questions remain. The researchers still need to determine whether large versions of the material will retain the same insulating properties and mechanical strength seen in the laboratory. Further testing must also establish how well the stacks tolerate repeated bending, accidental impacts, scratches, and other wear associated with real-world use.

If those challenges can be overcome, the technology could provide lightweight, flexible, durable insulation for lunar habitats, rovers, electronic equipment, and other systems operating in space.

For Levin, the results also offer a broader lesson about materials engineering. Even familiar products can reveal unexpected capabilities when researchers examine how their structures behave under different conditions.

"The simplest configuration ended up being the best one," she says.

The research was carried out at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science (Penn Engineering). Additional co-authors include Matthew F. Campbell, Gulzhan Aldan, and Orevaoghene H. Omodior.

Funding was provided by the National Science Foundation Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems (grant number 1845933) and Penn Engineering.

A biblical mystery, an ancient Egyptian inscription and a "ring of fire" solar eclipse 3,200 years ago hold clues to when Ramesses the Great ruled.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A total solar eclipse will sweep across the country, passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date.

We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps.

Astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it. When an ancient text reliably describes an eclipse, it can anchor a moment in history to a specific place and time.

We know from astronomical calculations that eclipses crossed Egypt long before anyone left an identifiable written record of one. On April 1, 2471 B.C., a total solar eclipse swept across northern Egypt during the age of the great pyramid builders. In research published in 2025, archaeoastronomer Giulio Magli at the Polytechnic University of Milan proposed that the eclipse may help explain why Pharaoh Shepseskaf broke with tradition and built a huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara instead of a pyramid. It's a tantalizing hypothesis, but no surviving Egyptian text records the eclipse.

Astronomers can calculate that an eclipse happened, but using it as a historical timestamp requires evidence that someone actually saw it and recorded it. That's where an eclipse almost 1,300 years later becomes particularly intriguing.

A passage in the Old Testament book of Joshua describes the sun and moon as if they stopped in the sky. After leading the people of Israel into Canaan — modern-day Israel and Palestine — Joshua prayed: "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies." Ancient Gibeon is about six miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.

In research published in 2017, researchers Colin Humphreys and Graeme Waddington at Cambridge University in the U.K. claimed it could refer to an annular solar eclipse on Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. It's a controversial interpretation, not least because it depends on exactly how the ancient Hebrew text is translated. However, if correct, it could be the oldest recorded solar eclipse with a date that has been identified — and it could also more accurately date the reign of Ramesses II. Also known as Ramesses the Great, he reigned for 66 years during Egypt's New Kingdom, commissioned Abu Simbel, made major additions to Karnak and Luxor Temple, and lived to be over 90. His reign marked the final peak of ancient Egyptian imperial power. According to the BBC, he is the "Jupiter" of the pharaonic system. However, the precise dates of his reign remain subject to debate, with historians using a combination of archaeological, historical and astronomical evidence to reconstruct the chronology.

Now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, the Merneptah Stele is a large inscribed granite monument written in the fifth year of Pharaoh Merneptah's reign, successor to Ramesses II. Discovered in 1896 at Merneptah's mortuary temple on the west bank of the Nile, opposite modern-day Luxor, it describes an Egyptian military campaign in Canaan and mentions Israelites. Egyptologists generally date Merneptah's reign to around 1213 — 1203 B.C., placing his fifth year around 1209/1208 B.C. That means the Israelites were already living in Canaan by then.

Using calculations that accounted for changes in Earth's rotation over thousands of years, Humphreys and Waddington identified an annular eclipse visible from Canaan for five minutes on the afternoon of Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. If the biblical passage does describe this event, that's a fixed astronomical date that could be used to refine the chronology of the Egyptian pharaohs. The researchers proposed that it occurred during the second, third or fourth year of Merneptah's reign.

If Humphreys and Waddington's interpretation of the biblical text is correct, the eclipse of 1207 B.C. could be the oldest solar eclipse identified in a written record. The researchers propose that Ramesses II reigned from approximately 1276 to 1210, with an uncertainty of about a year, slightly different from the conventional dates of 1279-1213 B.C. used by the British Museum.

So an eclipse can be like a timestamp on an undated photograph, but this one does not show that the book of Joshua actually describes an eclipse. The interpretation of the Hebrew has been challenged by Marinus Anthony van der Sluijs, whose paper argues that the biblical narrative states that the sun was standing over Gibeon and the moon was over the Valley of Aijalon simultaneously — so not an eclipse at all.

On Aug. 2, 2027, there will be no such ambiguity. We already know where the moon's shadow will cross Egypt, when it will reach Luxor and how long darkness will last. Almost 4,500 years separate that eclipse from the one that crossed Egypt in 2471 B.C. and 3,233 years from 1207 B.C., but both are movements of the same celestial clock. Run it forwards, and it predicts the future. Run it backward, and occasionally an eclipse of the sun can put a date on history.

#655. SXSW Forges Partnership With Egypt’s UTH Festival Dedicated to Youth Culture

Austin’s South by Southwest Film and TV Festival has forged a partnership with Egypt’s UTH Festival dedicated to youth culture under which UTH will become SXSW‘s partner in Egypt.

The agreement is aimed at “identifying emerging talent and building opportunities for Egyptian filmmakers, musicians, creators, founders and business leaders to engage with SXSW’s international network,” according to a statement. Related Stories Marvel’s ‘Blade’ Director Exited Failed Movie Because 'Life’s Too Short to Make S--- Films' and It Was 'Dangerous' Working 'Without a Proper Script' Mahershala Ali Says It ‘Doesn’t Matter’ That He’s Won 2 Oscars Because ‘There Are Not Roles for Me’ in ‘the Vast Majority of Projects’: ‘You’re Like Everybody Else Waiting’

The third edition of the just concluded UTH Festival just ran Nov. 20 and 21 at the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza, on the west bank of the Nile opposite Cairo, attracting roughly 10,000 attendees, according to organizers. This year’s festival, held under the theme “Work in Progress,” covered fashion, design, creator economy, film, music, food and sports, among other spheres.

The announcement stems from an initiative bringing SXSW and Egyptian industry figures together during the UTH fest, which was attended by Peter Lewis, who is SXSW’s chief commercial officer.

As part of the collaboration, an Egyptian delegation comprising roughly 20 participants will travel to SXSW to attend the fest between March 13–21. Curated and led by UTH, the delegation will “bring together representatives from Egypt’s film and music industries, the creator economy, entrepreneurship, investment and institutional sectors,” according to the statement. The agreement also includes plans for “a UTH-led programming session and a community gathering in Austin,” the statement added.

The collaboration also envisions possible Egyptian participation in the SXSW EDU program and SXSW London in 2027, with formats to be developed by the parties. Going forward, “UTH’s ambition is to establish an Egypt House at SXSW, providing a gathering place for Egyptian talent, companies and institutional partners in Austin,” according to the statement.

“SXSW was founded to help creative people connect, launch new ideas, and shape the future,” Peter Lewis said in the statement. “We are excited to partner with the UTH Festival team, who share our vision to empower the next generation of compelling, visionary and diverse creative voices,” he added. “We look forward to working closely with UTH in Egypt, and welcoming leaders from Egypt’s business, entertainment and creative industries to Austin next March.”

Commented Omar El Aawar, UTH Festival founder and CEO: “Egypt has no shortage of creative talent. What we need are more opportunities for that talent to connect with the global industry.”

El Aawar added: “Our partnership with SXSW is about building that bridge, creating real opportunities for Egyptian filmmakers, musicians, creators and entrepreneurs to take their work beyond our borders.”

“We want UTH to be more than a festival that brings people together for two days. We want to build a platform that opens doors throughout the year, and this partnership is an important step towards that ambition.”

#654. A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

Scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a new way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

To investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results showed that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

The second state was particularly important because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

"This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," says senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity."

A New Approach to Designing Quantum Materials

The discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely new electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

Future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open new possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

#653. Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

Should young people in Germany be more worried about their future than Baby Boomers were in the 1980s and 1990s? Or should both generations take to the streets and protest together? DW checked the data.

Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.

But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.

By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.

This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

Over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

He suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices."

This article was originally published in German.

Aldebaran looks for all the world like the brightest member of the Hyades star cluster. It isn't — and discovering why changes the way you look at constellations.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the big V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object.

Then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars. The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth. Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, while the Hyades are roughly 150 light-years distant. The orange eye of Taurus is a foreground star that happens to lie almost exactly along our line of sight toward the Hyades.

This fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing. The night sky looks flat, and our brains are extremely willing to believe it. But it has incredible depth — and when you can see parts of the night sky in 3D, that's when you begin to appreciate that you're not looking at a flat map. Instead, you begin to see our cosmic neighborhood as it really is. By appreciating depth, you learn its geography.

Taurus is now easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere during the evening. Once it's dark, look east for a small, tight knot of stars — the Pleiades open cluster (M45) — and then look nearby for a much larger V-shaped arrangement. That V is the Hyades, with unmistakably orange Aldebaran apparently sitting on one arm. Aldebaran's name is derived from the Arabic Al Dabarān, meaning "the follower," because it appears to trail the Pleiades across the night sky.

The Hyades is a real physical group of stars — an open cluster — that formed together and moves through our galaxy together. About 153 light-years away, the Hyades is the nearest open star cluster to Earth. The name means "the rainmakers" because their rising and setting times in the ancient Greek sky coincided with wet weather. The stars in the Hyades are of a similar age — and mostly sun-like stars, or similar — so astronomers can tell that they all formed together in the same nebula.

Orange-red star Aldebaran — the 14th-brightest star in the night sky — is the interloper, sitting less than half as far away from the sun. If you could somehow view the neighborhood from another part of the Milky Way, the familiar arrangement would fall apart. Aldebaran would no longer sit conveniently in the bull's face, and Taurus itself would stop looking like a bull.

Constellations aren't objects in the same sense as a planet or star cluster. They are merely views. Even stars that appear almost side by side can be separated by enormous distances. Our entire view of the night sky is a line-of-sight, 2D phenomenon — so all the patterns we see are an illusion.

Start with Aldebaran and the Hyades using only unaided eyes. Once you have the V, remind yourself of the distances — roughly 65 light-years for Aldebaran and 150 for the Hyades — and try to imagine pulling the orange star toward you while leaving the rest of the cluster behind. Stargazing like this can be much harder than it sounds. Even the brains of seasoned stargazers are hard-wired to find patterns of stars — constellations — and they rarely practice seeing stars at their correct distances.

Binoculars are worth using for the Hyades because the cluster is broad, so low magnification suits it well. Binoculars show many additional stars, but that's not really the point. Knowing what you're looking at changes the observation more than magnification does.

Trying to see the night sky in 3D is best done one constellation at a time, but I warn you — it makes you suspicious of everything. Next time you trace Orion, Cassiopeia or Auriga, you'll always be wondering which stars are nearby and which merely look that way. Looking up the distances and working it all out for yourself is an eye-opening experience.

Learning constellations gets you around the sky in a basic sense, but learning how to dismantle them and put them back together is when you begin to know the night sky as it really is.

This week is dominated by the moon. The moon is already waxing when the week begins and becomes the full Beaver Moon — a supermoon — on Nov. 24. That means progressively brighter evening skies and increasingly poor conditions for faint galaxies, nebulae and other low-contrast objects. Aldebaran and the main Hyades stars are bright enough to see from suburban skies even under strong moonlight, so you don't need to travel somewhere properly dark. Swapping your view from 2D to 3D takes only a little imagination. However, that could change in the few nights around the full moon — particularly on Nov. 23, when the waxing gibbous moon will move close to the nearby Pleiades, its strong light reducing the number of faint stars visible around them. Use binoculars to find some of its hundreds of stars.

I'm a stargazer and not at all interested in Greek mythology, but it sometimes helps to know a few basic ancient myths when finding constellations. A good example is the constellation Cepheus. It's named after a king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda — all three of which are close by in the northern sky right now. Look west after dark, away from the bright moon, to find the Summer Triangle — Vega, Deneb and Altair — which by now is sinking into the west. From Deneb, look north for a distinctive five-star pattern resembling a child's drawing of a house, with a square base and pointed roof. That's Cepheus. Its brightest star is Alderamin, about 49 light-years away, which marks one corner of the "house."

#651. James Gray on Francis Ford Coppola’s Advice That Shaped His Career: ‘Be Personal. There’s Only One of You in This World’

When filmmaker James Gray was a teenager, he wrote a fan letter to Francis Ford Coppola. To his surprise, the legendary filmmaker wrote back with a piece of advice that would come to shape Gray’s entire approach to cinema.

“He said, ‘Be personal, James. There’s only one of you in this world,’” Gray recalled during a press conference Sunday at the Doha Film Festival. “I’ve tried to take that to heart, that if I have anything to say at all, if I have a voice that matters at all, it’s best that I become as personal as I can.” Related Stories Marvel’s ‘Blade’ Director Exited Failed Movie Because 'Life’s Too Short to Make S--- Films' and It Was 'Dangerous' Working 'Without a Proper Script' Mahershala Ali Says It ‘Doesn’t Matter’ That He’s Won 2 Oscars Because ‘There Are Not Roles for Me’ in ‘the Vast Majority of Projects’: ‘You’re Like Everybody Else Waiting’

Decades later, that philosophy remains central to Gray’s filmmaking, even as he argues that the film industry increasingly pressures directors to suppress their individual voices.

“So much of the system, the systems in the cinema, both in the United States and abroad, try to discourage you from your own voice,” he said. “Or, if they don’t discourage you actively, they try to get you to bury your voice in a larger statement, or another form of genre, where it’s hidden.”

The director was in Doha to present the MENA premiere of “Paper Tiger,” his latest crime drama starring Adam Driver, Miles Teller and Scarlett Johansson. Set in 1980s New York, the film follows two brothers whose pursuit of the American Dream draws them into a dangerous scheme involving the Russian mafia.

Drawing heavily on his own family history, Gray described the film as an attempt to faithfully capture his father’s relationship with his uncle, while acknowledging the possible limitations of his own memory years later. He also recalled how a confrontation between his parents found its way into the film, with the actors recreating the incident almost exactly as it had unfolded in real life.

Although “Paper Tiger” is framed as a crime drama, Gray said he does not think of his films primarily in terms of genre, which he sees as a way of categorizing cinema rather than defining its true purpose.

“I’m just telling my story as best I can, as clearly as I can, as honestly as I can, and I hope for the best,” he said. For Gray, that commitment to honesty is also a means of fostering compassion and understanding. “That is how we extend the idea of compassion and sympathy in this world,” he explained. “Hopefully you can see something in me that matters to you.”

“I have been very lucky to be able to pursue a cinema which is very directly personal,” he added. “So I don’t take it lightly. It’s a responsibility I take very seriously. And I think it’s actually the true calling of the filmmaker.”

The conversation also turned to the future of independent cinema, with Brazilian producer Rodrigo Teixeira, whose “Paper Tiger” and “Furies” are both screening in Doha, pushing back against concerns about the dominance of Hollywood blockbusters.

“You’re always going to have space to create original films outside of the system, because it’s impossible to own the whole system, even with all these mergers,” Teixeira said, citing companies such as A24 and Neon as examples of how independent filmmaking continues to thrive.

Drawing a comparison between filmmaking in Brazil and the U.S., Teixeira argued that independent producers face much the same challenges regardless of geography. The principal difference, he said, is the public funding available in his home country, where federal support for cinema has long helped sustain the industry.

“We have a government who supports cinema, who supports art,” he said, contrasting Brazil’s system with the U.S., where comparable government support is absent.

Gray, meanwhile, recalled that he once believed cinema might follow the trajectory of opera, flourishing for roughly a century before eventually being eclipsed by another art form. While he acknowledged that cinema faces growing competition from video games and other forms of entertainment, and described the dominance of the blockbuster model as “overall quite harmful.” But the increasing accessibility of filmmaking technology has begun to challenge his earlier pessimism.

“I have a kind of optimism about the availability of technology and how that will introduce new voices.”

#650. Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.

Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity

The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

#649. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism showed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies

To explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies."

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

At first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

People with autism showed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

This increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research

The results raise important questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?"

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support."

The researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

Two of NASA's Mars explorers are sidelined by glitches at the moment.

The Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter have stood down from science work due to technical problems, NASA announced on Thursday (Nov. 19).

Perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna issue, and the venerable Odyssey is dealing with a balky reaction wheel. NASA hopes both can get back to work at Mars by the end of November.

Perseverance landed inside Mars' Jezero Crater in February 2021, tasked with assessing the area's potential to support past life and with collecting dozens of samples for future return to Earth.

It has done all this and more. The Perseverance team has determined that Jezero hosted a potentially habitable lake billions of years ago. And the car-sized rover has found a wealth of complex organic compounds in Martian rock, some of which might themselves be signs of life (though assessing this hypothesis fully will likely require bringing Perseverance's samples to Earth for analysis, scientists stress).

In addition, Perseverance just set a new distance record for off-Earth driving, rolling past the mark set by its smaller cousin, NASA's Opportunity rover (28.06 miles, or 45.16 kilometers).

Perseverance broke that record on Oct. 11. Just 19 days later, however, the mission team noticed a problem: The rover's main UHF downlink radio — which it uses to send information home to Earth, via data-relay satellites in Mars orbit — failed to send its usual "heartbeat" pings to the main computer.

Perseverance detected this problem autonomously and reacted as it was programmed to do: The six-wheeled robot switched to its backup UHF radio and went into a protective "safe mode," shutting down all non-essential systems.

The rover team recovered Perseverance from safe mode but soon noticed another issue: "The backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output," NASA officials wrote in an update on Thursday.

Perseverance's handlers have stopped using that backup radio as well; the rover is now communicating with Earth directly (without the help of relay orbiters), sending signals to NASA's Deep Space Network dishes via its high-gain antenna.

This pathway features lower data rates, and the mission team wants to prioritize the delivery of diagnostic information. So they've paused Perseverance's science work, which includes observations by its various cameras.

The glitch may be disappointing to devoted Perseverance fans, many of whom have already noticed that the mission website hasn't uploaded any new raw images since Nov. 7. But there's no reason to panic, according to NASA.

"The rover is stable and communicating with the team," agency officials wrote in Thursday's update. "The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November, and NASA will provide further updates in the future as the team works the issue."

Mars Odyssey's problem may be more serious: The orbiter, which arrived at the Red Planet in October 2001, recently lost the use of one of its reaction wheels.

Odyssey has four reaction wheels, which help the spacecraft maintain its orientation in space. Three of the four must be functional to do this job, and Odyssey already lost a reaction wheel in 2013.

This latest issue cropped up on Nov. 4, when Odyssey went into safe mode. The orbiter stayed in this protective posture until Nov. 6 while mission team members diagnosed and dealt with the problem. They've made some progress, at one point getting the faulty wheel to move when commanded.

"Further testing is being conducted to confirm whether the wheel is recoverable," NASA officials wrote in Thursday's update.

Though it has been out of safe mode for two weeks, Odyssey still has not resumed its science or data-relay work. (The orbiter has long helped NASA's Mars surface craft send information home to Earth.)

"The goal is for Odyssey to return to science and relay operations at the conclusion of these tests and analysis during the last week of November, and NASA will provide future updates on status and timeline as the team learns more," agency officials wrote in the update.

If the reaction wheel, isn't recoverable, Odyssey's days are numbered. The mission team will have to orient the orbiter solely using its thrusters, and Odyssey has enough hydrazine fuel left to do this for a just month or two, according to NASA.

Odyssey's mission has been a rousing success, no matter what happens with the reaction wheel. The orbiter has operated at Mars longer than any other spacecraft, and it has made a number of important scientific contributions.

"Odyssey created the first global maps detailing the composition of the Martian surface, which have become foundational for Mars geologists," NASA officials wrote in Thursday's update.

"The orbiter's surface maps have also played a key role in identifying hazards at landing sites, spotting locations of scientific interest for landers and rovers to explore, and mapping water molecules in the top 3 feet (1 meter) of the surface, including buried ice that could be useful to the first astronauts on Mars."

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#647. Turkey uses espionage accusations to pressure government critics

The arrest of a German foundation's employee in Istanbul this week has put the focus back on pressure tactics used by the Erdogan administration. The arrest is far from the first of its kind.

When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage.

But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of her German employer, the Heinrich Böll Foundation.

For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and the rights of women, minorities and LGBTQ+ people.

During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now also subject to a travel ban.

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. She is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the harshest critics of the current government.

Sik has recently been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefited members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and associates.

Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.

"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been leveled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like nongovernmental organizations and foundations.

Such accusations have often been followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. But what the many instances have in common is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.

In the past, such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

In 2015, for example, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.

In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.

Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.

Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, said the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argued. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.

"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law."

These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas said.

For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," he explained. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue."

In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.

It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas said.

The case of US pastor Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already made to stand trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.

In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. In the case of activist Osman Kavala, he was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.

But Tas said that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment."

This article was originally written in German.

#646. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," said Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction."

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy

The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life."

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

This variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray said. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships."

Like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict."

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she said. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions."
